note: Editorial, versioned event list for the Human History timeline. Years are astronomical integers (negative = BCE; no year zero adjustment is attempted for prehistory). datePrecision states how firm the date is; contested or approximate dates say so in the summary. `wikipedia` is the English article that anchors the event and supplies its image at build time. 195 events, deliberately balanced across regions.

events.title: Sahelanthropus, an early hominin, lives in Chad
events.summary: A skull nicknamed Toumaï, found in the Djurab Desert of Chad in 2001, belongs to Sahelanthropus tchadensis and is dated to roughly seven million years ago, close to the time the human and chimpanzee lineages separated. Whether it walked upright, and whether it sits on the human side of that split at all, is actively debated among palaeoanthropologists. It is placed here as the earliest candidate ancestor, not as a settled fact, and the date carries an uncertainty of hundreds of thousands of years.

events.title: Australopithecus afarensis walks upright
events.summary: The partial skeleton known as Lucy, found at Hadar in Ethiopia in 1974, and the fossil footprints preserved in volcanic ash at Laetoli in Tanzania show that Australopithecus afarensis walked habitually on two legs about 3.2 to 3.7 million years ago, while still having a small, ape-sized brain. Bipedalism therefore came long before large brains in human evolution. The species persisted for nearly a million years across East Africa and is a plausible, though not certain, ancestor of the genus Homo.

events.title: The first stone tools
events.summary: Deliberately flaked stone tools from Gona in Ethiopia are about 2.6 million years old, and cruder flaked stones from Lomekwi in Kenya may be 3.3 million years old, older than the genus Homo itself. The Oldowan toolkit of choppers and sharp flakes let hominins butcher carcasses and crack bones for marrow, opening a richer diet. Which species made the earliest tools is unresolved; what is clear is that tool-making predates and probably helped drive the growth of the human brain.

events.title: Homo erectus spreads across Africa and Asia
events.summary: Homo erectus appears in Africa about 1.9 million years ago and, within a few hundred thousand years, is found at Dmanisi in Georgia, in Java and in northern China, making it the first hominin known to leave Africa. Taller and longer-legged than earlier species, it made the symmetrical Acheulean hand axe and probably used fire. Populations in Indonesia survived until perhaps 100,000 years ago. Its dates and the boundaries between it and related species remain matters of specialist debate.

events.title: Habitual use of fire by early humans
events.wikipedia: Control of fire by early humans
events.summary: Hearths at sites such as Qesem Cave in Israel and Beeches Pit in England show hominins using fire habitually by about 400,000 years ago; claims for earlier, opportunistic use at Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa reach back a million years and remain debated. Cooking made more calories available from the same food and may have shaped the evolution of the human gut and brain. Fire also extended the day, warmed cold climates, and gave people a place to gather.

events.title: Neanderthals inhabit Europe and western Asia
events.summary: Neanderthals, a sister species to Homo sapiens, lived from at least 400,000 years ago until about 40,000 years ago across Europe and into Central Asia. They made complex tools, controlled fire, buried some of their dead and cared for injured members of their groups. They interbred with modern humans, and people outside Africa still carry about two percent Neanderthal ancestry. Why they disappeared is unsettled; competition, climate swings and small population size are all proposed.

events.title: Homo sapiens emerges in Africa
events.summary: The earliest fossils widely accepted as Homo sapiens come from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, dated to roughly 300,000 years ago, with later finds at Omo Kibish and Herto in Ethiopia. The date is a genuine estimate: it depends on thermoluminescence dating of burnt flints and on where researchers draw the line between archaic and modern anatomy. What is not contested is the geography. Every line of fossil and genetic evidence places the origin of our species in Africa, from which all later dispersals began.

events.title: Engraved ochre at Blombos Cave
events.summary: At Blombos Cave on South Africa's southern coast, people engraved cross-hatched patterns on pieces of red ochre and strung shell beads around 75,000 years ago, and mixed ochre paint in abalone shells about 100,000 years ago. These are among the oldest known signs of symbolic thought and decoration, well before the famous cave art of Europe. They show that behaviour we call fully modern arose in Africa, in step with the anatomy, rather than in a later European burst.

events.title: Modern humans spread out of Africa
events.wikipedia: Early expansions of hominins out of Africa
events.summary: Genetic evidence points to a major dispersal of Homo sapiens out of Africa between roughly 70,000 and 50,000 years ago, from which most non-African populations descend, though earlier and smaller excursions into the Levant and perhaps beyond are attested by fossils. Along the way these people met and interbred with Neanderthals and Denisovans. By around 50,000 years ago they had reached Australia, a crossing that required open-water voyaging and is among the earliest evidence of seafaring.

events.title: People reach Australia by sea
events.summary: Humans reached Australia at least 50,000 years ago, and finds at Madjedbebe rock shelter in Arnhem Land are argued to push the date to 65,000 years, a claim still debated. Getting there required crossing open sea between the islands of Wallacea, the earliest known deliberate ocean voyages. The descendants of those settlers, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, maintain the longest continuous cultural traditions on Earth, recorded in rock art, song and land management.

events.title: The oldest known figurative cave art, Sulawesi
events.summary: A life-sized painting of a warty pig in the cave of Leang Tedongnge on Sulawesi, Indonesia, has been dated by uranium-series analysis of overlying mineral crusts to at least 45,500 years ago, and a hunting scene in nearby Leang Bulu' Sipong to about 44,000 years. These predate the celebrated paintings of Chauvet and Lascaux in France and show that figurative art existed in island Southeast Asia as early as anywhere. The dates are minimums; the paintings could be older.

events.title: People enter the Americas
events.summary: Humans moved from Siberia into the Americas across or along the coast of Beringia during the last glacial period. Sites such as Monte Verde in Chile, about 14,500 years old, show that people were far south before the ice-free corridor opened, and footprints at White Sands, New Mexico, have been dated to around 21,000 to 23,000 years ago, a claim still being tested. The route, timing and number of migrations remain among the liveliest questions in archaeology.

events.title: Early pottery in East Asia and the Jōmon
events.summary: The world's oldest known pottery comes from Xianrendong Cave in China, about 20,000 years old, and from Japan, where the Jōmon culture was making cord-marked vessels by about 14,000 BCE, thousands of years before farming reached the archipelago. Pots allowed foods to be boiled and stored, changing diets and settlement. The Jōmon people remained largely hunter-gatherer-fishers for ten millennia, and their elaborate later vessels and clay figurines are among the earliest sustained ceramic art traditions.

events.title: Farming begins in the Fertile Crescent
events.summary: In the hills of the Fertile Crescent people began cultivating wheat, barley, lentils and peas and herding sheep and goats around 9500 BCE. Farming arose independently several times elsewhere, including rice in the Yangtze valley, maize in Mesoamerica, and millet, squash and potatoes in other regions, so no single origin is meant here. Agriculture allowed permanent villages and larger populations, but early farmers were often shorter and less healthy than the foragers they replaced.

events.title: Göbekli Tepe, monumental building before farming
events.summary: On a hilltop in southeastern Turkey, hunter-gatherers raised circles of carved limestone pillars, some over five metres tall and weighing ten tonnes, beginning around 9500 BCE, before pottery, metal or, on most readings, agriculture. The site overturned the assumption that monumental architecture and organised religion followed farming rather than preceding it. Its purpose is debated; interpretations range from a ritual centre for scattered bands to a settlement whose domestic areas are only now being excavated.

events.title: Maize is domesticated in Mesoamerica
events.summary: In the Balsas River valley of southern Mexico, people transformed teosinte, a grass with a few hard kernels, into maize around 9,000 years ago, one of the most dramatic domestications in agriculture. Maize spread north and south through the Americas, supporting the Olmec, Maya, Aztec and Inca civilisations and, after 1492, feeding much of Africa, Europe and Asia. Its nixtamalisation with lime, a Mesoamerican invention, made its niacin available and prevented pellagra.

events.title: Rice is domesticated in the Yangtze valley
events.summary: Farmers in the lower Yangtze valley of China were cultivating rice by around 7000 BCE, and genetic evidence suggests domesticated Oryza sativa japonica arose from wild rice there, with indica rice developing later in South Asia through crossing. Rice became the staple of more people than any other crop and the basis of the dense, irrigated societies of East and Southeast Asia. The dates come from charred grains and phytoliths and are approximate to a millennium.

events.title: The wheel and the wheeled vehicle
events.summary: Potter's wheels were in use in Mesopotamia by about 3500 BCE, and the earliest evidence for wheeled vehicles appears almost simultaneously in Mesopotamia, the Caucasus and central Europe, including a pictograph from Uruk, wagon models and the Bronocice pot from Poland. Where the vehicle wheel was first invented is unknown. Drawn by oxen and later horses, carts and chariots transformed farming, trade and war, though the Americas, lacking draught animals, did without them until 1492.

events.title: Bronze metallurgy spreads
events.summary: Alloying copper with tin to make bronze, harder and easier to cast than either, was practised in Mesopotamia and the Iranian plateau by about 3300 BCE, and later independently in China, where the Shang dynasty cast ritual vessels of unmatched complexity. Because tin was scarce, bronze drove long-distance trade networks from Cornwall and Afghanistan to the Aegean. Bronze weapons and tools defined an age that ended, in the eastern Mediterranean, in a wave of collapses around 1200 BCE.

events.title: Writing is invented in Mesopotamia
events.summary: Clay tablets from Uruk in southern Mesopotamia record goods and rations in a proto-cuneiform script from about 3200 BCE, the earliest writing system that can be read. Egyptian hieroglyphs appear at nearly the same time, and writing was invented again, independently, in China and in Mesoamerica. Writing began as bookkeeping and only later carried literature, law and history. Because it allows knowledge to outlive its authors, it is the conventional boundary between prehistory and history.

events.title: Caral and the first cities of the Americas
events.summary: At Caral in the Supe valley of Peru, monumental platform mounds, sunken plazas and residential districts were built from about 2600 BCE, contemporary with the pyramids of Egypt and older than any other urban centre in the Americas. The Norte Chico or Caral-Supe culture grew cotton for fishing nets and traded with the coast; it left no pottery and no evidence of warfare. Knotted-cord quipu found there hint at a recording system millennia before the Inca.

events.title: Cities of the Indus Valley civilisation
events.summary: Between about 2600 and 1900 BCE cities such as Mohenjo-daro and Harappa, in present-day Pakistan and northwest India, housed tens of thousands of people on planned grids with baked-brick houses, covered drains, public baths and standardised weights. Its script, on thousands of seals, remains undeciphered, so its rulers, gods and language are unknown. The civilisation declined as rivers shifted and monsoons weakened; its people did not vanish but dispersed into smaller settlements.

events.title: The Great Pyramid of Giza is built
events.summary: Built for the pharaoh Khufu around 2560 BCE, the Great Pyramid stood as the tallest human-made structure on Earth for nearly four thousand years. Its roughly 2.3 million blocks were quarried, moved and set with copper tools, ramps, levers and a large, organised, paid workforce housed in a nearby town, not by enslaved labour as once assumed. The precision of its alignment to the cardinal points shows Old Kingdom Egypt commanded advanced surveying and administration.

events.title: Stonehenge's sarsen circle is raised
events.summary: The great sarsen stones of Stonehenge, on Salisbury Plain in England, were raised around 2500 BCE within an earlier earthwork begun about 3000 BCE; the smaller bluestones were hauled from the Preseli hills of Wales, 250 kilometres away. The monument is aligned on the midsummer sunrise and midwinter sunset, and burials show it was a place of the dead. Its builders left no writing, so its exact meaning is unknown, but it is the best-studied of Europe's Neolithic megaliths.

events.title: The Code of Hammurabi
events.summary: Hammurabi, king of Babylon, had nearly three hundred legal rulings carved on a basalt stele around 1755 BCE, covering contracts, wages, property, family and injury. It is not the oldest law code, but it is the longest and best preserved from the ancient Near East, and it is publicly displayed law, meant to be seen. Its principle that the strong should not oppress the weak, stated in the prologue, sits beside penalties that varied sharply by social class.

events.title: The Lapita people settle the western Pacific
events.summary: Between about 1500 and 900 BCE seafarers making distinctive dentate-stamped pottery spread from the Bismarck Archipelago east through the Solomons, Vanuatu, New Caledonia, Fiji, Tonga and Samoa, the first people to reach these islands. Their ancestry combined Austronesian speakers from Taiwan and island Southeast Asia with Papuan populations. Carrying pigs, dogs, chickens, taro and yams in outrigger canoes, the Lapita are the ancestors of the Polynesians, whose later voyages settled the remote Pacific.

events.title: The Vedas are composed
events.summary: The Rigveda, a collection of over a thousand hymns in an early form of Sanskrit, was composed in the northwest of the Indian subcontinent between about 1500 and 1200 BCE and transmitted orally with extraordinary precision for many centuries before being written down. The later Vedas, Brahmanas and Upanishads, composed down to about 500 BCE, developed ritual, philosophy and the ideas of karma and rebirth. They form the oldest scriptural layer of Hinduism, the world's third-largest religion.

events.title: Ironworking becomes widespread
events.summary: Smelted iron was known in Anatolia by the second millennium BCE, and after about 1200 BCE, as Mediterranean trade in tin faltered, iron tools and weapons spread through the Near East, India and Europe. Iron ore is common, so metal tools became cheap enough for ordinary farmers. Sub-Saharan Africa developed ironworking on its own, with furnaces in Nigeria, Rwanda and Tanzania dated to the first millennium BCE, a chronology still being refined by new excavations.

events.title: The Olmec civilisation flourishes
events.summary: Along the Gulf coast of Mexico the Olmec built ceremonial centres at San Lorenzo and La Venta from about 1200 BCE, carving colossal basalt heads and creating a religious imagery of jaguars and rulers that later Mesoamerican peoples inherited. They may have devised the ritual ballgame and early forms of the Long Count calendar and writing, though the earliest datable examples come from their successors. Often called Mesoamerica's mother culture, a label archaeologists debate.

events.title: The Phoenician alphabet
events.summary: Merchants of the Levantine coast standardised a script of 22 consonant letters around 1050 BCE, descended from earlier Semitic signs used by Canaanite workers in Egypt's Sinai mines. Because it needed only a couple of dozen symbols rather than hundreds, it could be learned quickly. Carried on Phoenician ships, it was adapted by the Greeks, who added vowels, and from them by the Etruscans and Romans; Aramaic, Hebrew, Arabic and the Brahmi scripts of India descend from the same family.

events.title: Zoroaster and the origins of Zoroastrianism
events.summary: Zoroaster, the prophet of ancient Iran whose hymns, the Gathas, form the core of the Avesta, is dated by scholars anywhere between about 1500 and 600 BCE; the language of the Gathas suggests the earlier end. His teaching of one creator god, Ahura Mazda, a cosmic struggle between truth and lie, individual judgment and a final renewal of the world influenced Judaism, Christianity and Islam. Zoroastrianism was the state religion of three Persian empires.

events.title: Chavín de Huántar and early Andean civilisation
events.summary: High in the Peruvian Andes, the ceremonial centre of Chavín de Huántar drew pilgrims from across the region between about 900 and 200 BCE to a temple of stone galleries, water channels and carved deities combining jaguar, serpent and human features. Its religious art and iconography spread widely, an early instance of the cultural unification of the Andes that the Inca would later complete politically. Metalworking in gold and textile technology advanced during the same centuries.

events.title: Judaism and the Hebrew Bible take shape
events.summary: The religion of ancient Israel developed into Judaism, centred on one God and the Torah, during and after the Babylonian exile of the sixth century BCE, when much of the Hebrew Bible reached the form we know; scholars date its final editing to the Persian period, around 500 to 400 BCE. Traditions of Abraham and Moses are far older but cannot be dated historically. Judaism's scriptures, ethics and monotheism underlie Christianity and Islam.

events.title: The Cyrus Cylinder
events.summary: After capturing Babylon in 539 BCE, Cyrus the Great of Persia had a clay cylinder inscribed in Akkadian recording his restoration of temples and the return of displaced peoples to their homelands, a policy the Hebrew Bible credits with ending the Jewish exile. It follows Mesopotamian conventions of royal proclamation rather than declaring universal rights, and its modern reputation as the first charter of human rights is disputed by historians. It remains a notable early statement of religious tolerance by a conqueror.

events.title: Cleisthenes founds Athenian democracy
events.summary: In 508 BCE the Athenian reformer Cleisthenes reorganised the citizen body into ten tribes and gave the assembly of all adult male citizens the final say over law and war, creating the system later called democracy. Offices were filled by lot, and juries of hundreds judged cases. It excluded women, slaves and resident foreigners, a majority of the population, yet its principle that citizens rule themselves directly became a reference point for every later republic.

events.title: Confucius teaches in China
events.summary: Kong Qiu, known in the West as Confucius, taught in the state of Lu during the late sixth and early fifth centuries BCE, in a period of political fragmentation. His emphasis on ritual propriety, filial duty, learning and humane government was compiled by followers in the Analects. Adopted as state doctrine under the Han dynasty, Confucian thought organised education, the civil service examinations and family life in China for two millennia and deeply influenced Korea, Japan and Vietnam.

events.title: Siddhartha Gautama teaches; Buddhism begins
events.summary: Siddhartha Gautama, later the Buddha, taught in the Ganges plain of northern India in about the fifth century BCE; scholars place his death anywhere between roughly 480 and 400 BCE, so the century is firm and the decades are not. His teaching of a middle path, the four noble truths and release from suffering spread across Asia along trade routes, taking distinct Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana forms and shaping the art, ethics and politics of dozens of societies.

events.title: The Greco-Persian Wars
events.summary: Between 499 and 449 BCE the Achaemenid Persian Empire, the largest state the world had yet seen, fought the Greek city-states. Persian invasions were turned back at Marathon in 490 and, after the sacrifice at Thermopylae, at sea off Salamis in 480 and on land at Plataea in 479. The wars gave Athens its navy and its empire, and Herodotus's account of them is the first surviving work of history. Persia remained the dominant power of the Near East for another 150 years.

events.title: Hippocratic medicine
events.summary: Hippocrates of Kos and the physicians who wrote under his name around 400 BCE treated disease as a natural process with natural causes, to be understood by careful observation of the patient rather than attributed to the gods. The Hippocratic Corpus describes case histories, prognosis and the ethics later distilled into the Hippocratic Oath. Its humoral theory was wrong, and persisted for two thousand years, but its method of observation and its professional ethics are the roots of clinical medicine.

events.title: Alexander the Great's conquests
events.summary: In eleven years from 334 BCE Alexander of Macedon destroyed the Persian Empire, took Egypt, marched through Central Asia and fought in the Punjab before his army refused to go further. He died in Babylon in 323 aged 32, and his generals carved his conquests into kingdoms. The Hellenistic world they ruled spread Greek language, cities, science and art from the Mediterranean to Afghanistan, and brought Greek and Indian, Persian and Egyptian ideas into lasting contact.

events.title: Euclid's Elements
events.summary: Working in Alexandria around 300 BCE, Euclid organised the geometry and number theory of earlier Greek mathematicians into thirteen books that begin from definitions, postulates and common notions and prove each proposition from what came before. The Elements set the standard of mathematical proof and was the basic geometry textbook for over two thousand years, in Greek, Arabic, Latin and every modern language. Almost nothing is known of Euclid himself; even his dates are inferred.

events.title: The Punic Wars
events.summary: Rome and Carthage fought three wars between 264 and 146 BCE for control of the western Mediterranean. In the second, Hannibal crossed the Alps with elephants and destroyed Roman armies at Cannae, yet Rome refused to yield and won in Africa at Zama in 202. The third ended with Carthage razed and its territory made a Roman province. Victory left Rome the dominant power of the Mediterranean and set it on the road from republic to empire.

events.title: Ashoka's edicts
events.summary: After the bloody conquest of Kalinga around 260 BCE, the Mauryan emperor Ashoka renounced war and had edicts carved on rocks and pillars across the Indian subcontinent, from Afghanistan to the Deccan, in Prakrit, Greek and Aramaic. They proclaim dhamma, a policy of non-violence, religious tolerance, care for the sick, prisoners and animals, and just administration, and describe the emperor's own remorse. They are the earliest surviving royal inscriptions of India and a rare ancient statement of governance by ethical principle.

events.title: Archimedes and the mathematics of machines
events.summary: Archimedes of Syracuse, who died when the Romans took the city in 212 BCE, worked out the law of the lever, the principle of buoyancy that bears his name, the volume and surface of the sphere, and a method of exhaustion that anticipated integral calculus. He designed compound pulleys and the water-raising screw and, by tradition, war machines to defend Syracuse. His surviving treatises, recovered partly from a palimpsest, show a mathematical physicist working eighteen centuries before Galileo.

events.title: Qin Shi Huang unifies China
events.summary: In 221 BCE the king of Qin completed the conquest of the six rival Warring States and proclaimed himself Qin Shi Huang, First Emperor. He standardised the script, weights, measures, coinage and axle widths, built roads and canals, linked earlier walls into a northern frontier, and was buried with the terracotta army near Xi'an. His dynasty fell four years after his death, but the unified, centrally administered empire he created became the enduring shape of China.

events.title: Zhang Qian and the opening of the Silk Road
events.summary: Sent west by the Han emperor Wu in 138 BCE to seek allies against the Xiongnu, the envoy Zhang Qian was captured, escaped, and returned thirteen years later with the first Chinese accounts of Central Asia, Bactria and Persia. His reports led the Han to push into the Tarim Basin and open regular trade with the west. The routes later called the Silk Road carried silk, horses, glass, religions, technologies and, at times, plague between China, India, Persia and Rome.

events.title: Julius Caesar is assassinated; the Roman Empire follows
events.summary: Julius Caesar, who had crossed the Rubicon in 49 BCE and won a civil war to become dictator, was stabbed to death by senators on the Ides of March, 44 BCE. His death did not restore the republic: thirteen more years of civil war ended with his heir Octavian defeating Antony and Cleopatra and taking the name Augustus in 27 BCE as the first emperor. The Roman Empire he founded ruled the Mediterranean world for the next four centuries.

events.title: The ministry of Jesus; Christianity begins
events.summary: Jesus of Nazareth taught in Galilee and Judea and was executed by the Roman authorities in Jerusalem around 30 CE; the exact year is uncertain within a few years either side. His followers, first a movement within Judaism, spread his message through the Roman Empire, aided by Paul's letters and the Greek-speaking cities of the eastern Mediterranean. Three centuries later Christianity was tolerated and then adopted by the empire, becoming the largest religion in the world today.

events.title: Teotihuacan rises
events.summary: Northeast of modern Mexico City, Teotihuacan grew after 100 CE into one of the largest cities in the world, with perhaps 100,000 people, a grid plan, the Pyramids of the Sun and Moon and apartment compounds housing craft workers and migrants from across Mesoamerica. Its influence reached the Maya cities, where its warriors intervened in 378. The city burned around 550 in circumstances still debated. Its builders' name for it and their language are unknown.

events.title: Papermaking is perfected in Han China
events.summary: The court official Cai Lun reported an improved papermaking process to the Han emperor in 105 CE, using bark, hemp, rags and fishing nets; archaeology shows cruder paper in China a century or two earlier, so he standardised rather than invented it. Paper was far cheaper than silk or bamboo strips and spread with Buddhism to Korea and Japan, reached the Islamic world after 751, and Europe by the twelfth century, where it made printing economical.

events.title: Ptolemy's Almagest
events.summary: Claudius Ptolemy, working in Alexandria around 150 CE, compiled Greek and Babylonian astronomy into a mathematical model of an Earth-centred cosmos that predicted planetary positions well enough to remain the standard for 1,400 years, in Greek, Arabic and Latin. His Geography, with its coordinates of thousands of places, guided mapmakers into the age of Columbus. The Almagest was wrong about the Earth's place, but its demand that theory match measured positions made it the model of quantitative science.

events.title: The Classic Maya and their collapse
events.summary: Between about 250 and 900 CE Maya city-states such as Tikal, Calakmul, Copán and Palenque raised stone pyramids, recorded their kings' wars and rituals in the only fully developed writing system of the pre-Columbian Americas, and computed calendars and astronomical cycles with great precision. In the ninth century the southern lowland cities were abandoned one after another; drought, warfare, overpopulation and political failure are all implicated, in a mix still debated. Maya society continued in the north and survives today.

events.title: The Kingdom of Aksum adopts Christianity
events.summary: Aksum, in the highlands of present-day Ethiopia and Eritrea, controlled Red Sea trade between Rome and India, minted its own gold coins and raised carved granite stelae over thirty metres tall. Around 330 CE King Ezana converted to Christianity, making Aksum one of the first states to adopt the faith, a decade or so after Armenia and before the Roman Empire did officially. The Ethiopian Orthodox Church, with its own script and scriptures, descends directly from this decision.

events.title: The Western Roman Empire ends
events.wikipedia: Fall of the Western Roman Empire
events.summary: In 476 the Germanic general Odoacer deposed the boy emperor Romulus Augustulus and sent the imperial insignia to Constantinople, the date conventionally taken as the end of the Western Roman Empire after a century of invasions, civil wars and fiscal decline. Historians stress that the transition was gradual: Roman law, cities, Latin and the Church persisted under the Gothic, Frankish and other kingdoms, and the Eastern Empire continued from Constantinople for another thousand years.

events.title: Indian mathematicians develop the decimal place-value system and zero
events.summary: Indian mathematicians of the Gupta era and after wrote numbers with ten symbols in place-value notation, and in 628 CE Brahmagupta's Brahmasphutasiddhanta gave rules for arithmetic with zero as a number in its own right, including negative numbers and debts. The Bakhshali manuscript, whose leaves have been radiocarbon-dated to between the third and tenth centuries, contains an early dot for zero. Transmitted through the Islamic world, these became the Hindu-Arabic numerals used everywhere today.

events.title: Tiwanaku on the Bolivian altiplano
events.summary: Near the southern shore of Lake Titicaca, nearly 4,000 metres above sea level, Tiwanaku grew between about 500 and 1000 CE into a city of monumental platforms, the Gateway of the Sun and precisely fitted stonework, supported by raised-field agriculture that kept crops from freezing. Its influence, with that of contemporary Wari to the north, reached across Bolivia, Peru and Chile. Prolonged drought around 1000 is thought to have brought its decline. The Inca later claimed it as their origin place.

events.title: The Corpus Juris Civilis of Justinian
events.summary: The emperor Justinian ordered Roman law collected, edited and systematised; the Code, Digest and Institutes issued between 529 and 534 preserved a thousand years of Roman legal thought in a form students and courts could use. Rediscovered in Italy in the eleventh century, the Corpus became the foundation of the civil-law systems of continental Europe, Latin America and much of Asia and Africa, and of canon law. Concepts such as contract, property and legal personhood descend from it.

events.title: The Plague of Justinian
events.summary: The first recorded pandemic of bubonic plague reached Egypt in 541 and Constantinople in 542, where the historian Procopius described thousands dying daily. Ancient DNA has confirmed the bacterium Yersinia pestis in graves from the period. Older estimates of mortality in the tens of millions have been challenged by recent scholarship, which finds less evidence of demographic collapse than once assumed. Recurrent outbreaks continued until about 750, forming the First Plague Pandemic.

events.title: Muhammad's revelations; Islam begins
events.summary: According to Islamic tradition, Muhammad received his first revelation near Mecca in 610 CE and continued to receive the verses later compiled as the Quran until his death in 632. His migration to Medina in 622 marks year one of the Islamic calendar. Within a century of his death Muslim rule stretched from Spain to the Indus, and the faith's law, scholarship, architecture and trade networks linked Africa, Asia and Europe for the next thousand years.

events.title: The Tang dynasty and Chang'an
events.summary: The Tang dynasty, founded in 618, ruled a China open to the world: its capital Chang'an, with about a million people, was probably the largest city on Earth, home to Persian, Sogdian, Turkic and Indian merchants, Buddhist monks, Nestorian Christians and Muslims. Tang armies reached the Pamirs; Tang poetry, law codes and administration were adopted in Japan, Korea and Vietnam. Woodblock printing appeared in this era. The dynasty declined after the An Lushan rebellion of 755 and fell in 907.

events.title: The early Muslim conquests
events.summary: Within a century of Muhammad's death in 632, Arab armies under the Rashidun and Umayyad caliphs had taken Syria, Egypt and Persia, crossed North Africa into Spain, and reached the Indus and the Talas river in Central Asia. The Sasanian Empire was destroyed and the Byzantine Empire halved. Conquest was not mass conversion; Christians, Jews and Zoroastrians paid a tax and kept their faiths, and Islam became the majority religion in most of these lands only over centuries.

events.title: Japan's first histories and the Nara court
events.summary: The Kojiki of 712 and Nihon Shoki of 720, compiled at the imperial court, recorded the myths of the kami, the sun goddess Amaterasu and the descent of the imperial line, fixing in writing the traditions later called Shinto, alongside Chinese-style chronicles. The court at Nara, laid out on the model of Chang'an, sponsored Buddhism as well: the Great Buddha of Tōdai-ji was dedicated in 752. Japan's dual religious tradition of kami and Buddhas dates from this century.

events.title: Borobudur and the Buddhist kingdoms of Java and Sumatra
events.summary: The Sailendra rulers of central Java built Borobudur, the world's largest Buddhist monument, around 780 to 830 CE: a stepped pyramid of nine terraces carrying 2,672 relief panels and 504 Buddha statues, arranged as a pilgrim's path from the world of desire to enlightenment. Contemporary Srivijaya on Sumatra controlled the straits between India and China and was a centre of Buddhist learning visited by Chinese pilgrims. Both show Southeast Asia adapting Indian religion into its own monumental forms.

events.title: Charlemagne is crowned emperor
events.summary: On Christmas Day 800 Pope Leo III crowned Charles, king of the Franks, as emperor in Rome, the first in the West since 476. Charlemagne's wars had joined France, Germany and northern Italy under one rule and forced the Saxons into Christianity; his court at Aachen gathered scholars who revived Latin learning and copied the classical texts that survive today. His empire split among his grandsons, but the ideas of a Christian empire and of the Franks as heirs of Rome shaped medieval Europe.

events.title: Baghdad's House of Wisdom and Al-Khwarizmi's algebra
events.summary: Under the Abbasid caliph al-Ma'mun, scholars in Baghdad translated Greek, Persian and Indian works into Arabic and built on them. Around 820 Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi wrote a treatise on solving equations whose title gave the world the word algebra and, in a second book, explained the Indian decimal numerals; a Latin corruption of his name gave us algorithm. Arabic became the language of science from Spain to Central Asia for four centuries.

events.title: Gunpowder is invented in China
events.summary: Chinese alchemists seeking an elixir of immortality recorded a mixture of saltpetre, sulphur and charcoal that burned violently in a Taoist text of about 850 CE. By 1044 the Song dynasty's military manual gave gunpowder recipes, and over the next two centuries the Chinese developed fire arrows, bombs, rockets, and the first true guns. Through the Mongols and the Islamic world, gunpowder reached Europe by the late thirteenth century, where cannon would end the age of castles.

events.title: Song China's economic and technological revolution
events.summary: Song China, from 960 to 1279, was the most advanced economy in the world: it issued the first paper money, produced iron on a scale Europe would not match for seven centuries, built ocean-going junks with watertight compartments, and its cities of Kaifeng and Hangzhou passed a million inhabitants. Shen Kuo described the magnetic compass and fossils; Su Song built an astronomical clock tower. Civil service examinations drew officials from a broad gentry. The Mongols conquered the Song in 1279.

events.title: The Christianisation of Kievan Rus'
events.summary: In 988 Vladimir the Great, prince of Kiev, accepted baptism from Constantinople, married a Byzantine princess and had his people baptised in the Dnieper, choosing Orthodox Christianity over Islam, Judaism and Latin Christianity according to the Primary Chronicle's famous story. The decision bound the East Slavs to the Byzantine world, its Cyrillic script, church architecture and law. Russia, Ukraine and Belarus all trace their religious and cultural origins to this event, and compete over its legacy.

events.title: Polynesians settle the remote Pacific
events.summary: Sailing double-hulled canoes and navigating by stars, swells, birds and cloud, Polynesian voyagers settled the islands of the eastern Pacific in a final burst between about 1000 and 1280 CE: the Society Islands, Hawaii, Rapa Nui (Easter Island) and, last, Aotearoa New Zealand. Radiocarbon dates have compressed this expansion to a few centuries, far later than once thought. It was the last great settlement of uninhabited land by humans and the most remarkable feat of pre-modern navigation.

events.title: The Swahili city-states of the East African coast
events.summary: From about 1000 CE, Kilwa, Mombasa, Zanzibar, Sofala and other stone-built towns along the East African coast linked the interior's gold, ivory and slaves to the monsoon trade of the Indian Ocean, with Arab, Persian, Indian and Chinese partners. Their people spoke Swahili, a Bantu language with Arabic loanwords, and were Muslim from the eleventh century. Kilwa minted its own coins and Ibn Battuta praised it in 1331. The Portuguese sacked the coast after 1505.

events.title: Ibn al-Haytham founds the science of optics
events.summary: Working in Cairo, Ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen) completed his Book of Optics around 1021, showing by experiment that vision occurs when light reflected from objects enters the eye, refuting the ancient theory of rays emitted by the eye, and describing the camera obscura, refraction and the anatomy of the eye. His insistence on testing hypotheses by controlled experiment has earned him a claim to be the first modern scientist. Translated into Latin, his work influenced Kepler and the development of lenses.

events.title: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine
events.summary: Ibn Sina, known in Latin as Avicenna, born near Bukhara, completed his Canon of Medicine in 1025, a five-volume synthesis of Greek, Persian and Indian medicine organised systematically, with sections on anatomy, diseases, drugs and the testing of remedies. Translated into Latin in the twelfth century, it was a standard medical textbook in European universities into the seventeenth century and in the Islamic world longer. His philosophical works were equally influential on scholastic thought.

events.title: Bi Sheng invents movable type
events.summary: Between 1039 and 1048 the artisan Bi Sheng made individual characters of baked clay, set them in a frame with wax and resin, printed, and then reused them, as the polymath Shen Kuo recorded in his Dream Pool Essays. Woodblock printing, older and better suited to thousands of Chinese characters, remained dominant in China, but movable type was developed further in Korea, where the Jikji of 1377 is the oldest surviving book printed with metal type, seven decades before Gutenberg.

events.title: The magnetic compass is used for navigation
events.summary: Chinese texts of the eleventh century describe magnetised needles floating in water to indicate south, first for geomancy, and Zhu Yu's Pingzhou Table Talks of 1117 records their use by ship pilots at sea, the earliest clear evidence of navigation by compass. Within a century the instrument appears in Arabic and European sources, probably transmitted along the maritime routes of the Indian Ocean. Together with the sternpost rudder and watertight bulkheads, also Chinese, it made long ocean voyages routine.

events.title: Cahokia, the largest city north of Mexico
events.summary: Around 1050 CE a settlement near present-day St. Louis grew rapidly into Cahokia, a planned city of perhaps 10,000 to 20,000 people with more than a hundred earthen mounds, the largest, Monks Mound, covering as much ground as the Great Pyramid. Its Mississippian culture, based on maize, spread its art and religion across the eastern United States. The city was abandoned by about 1350, for reasons that may include floods, drought and political breakdown, and its builders' name is unknown.

events.title: The first universities
events.summary: The University of Bologna, traditionally dated to 1088, was the first institution to grant degrees recognised beyond its own city; Paris and Oxford followed within a century. Older centres of higher learning existed elsewhere, notably al-Qarawiyyin in Fez, founded in 859, and al-Azhar in Cairo, and Buddhist Nalanda in India. The European university's distinctive features, self-governing guilds of masters and students and formal degrees, spread with colonialism to become the worldwide model.

events.title: The First Crusade
events.summary: Answering Pope Urban II's call at Clermont in 1095, tens of thousands of western Europeans marched east, massacred Jewish communities in the Rhineland on the way, and in July 1099 stormed Jerusalem, slaughtering much of its Muslim and Jewish population. They founded crusader states that lasted until 1291. Eight more major crusades followed over two centuries, embittering relations between Christians and Muslims, and between Latin and Greek Christians after the sack of Constantinople in 1204.

events.title: Great Zimbabwe is built
events.summary: From about 1100 CE the Shona built Great Zimbabwe, a city of dry-stone walls, the largest of which, the Great Enclosure, stands eleven metres high with a perimeter of 250 metres, laid without mortar. The city of perhaps 18,000 people controlled gold and ivory trade to the Swahili coast; Chinese porcelain and Persian glass have been found there. Colonial-era writers denied its African origin; archaeology has long established it. It was abandoned around 1450 as trade routes shifted.

events.title: Angkor Wat is built by the Khmer Empire
events.summary: King Suryavarman II of the Khmer Empire built Angkor Wat in present-day Cambodia in the first half of the twelfth century as a Hindu temple to Vishnu, the largest religious monument in the world by land area. Its five towers represent Mount Meru; its galleries carry over a kilometre of bas-reliefs. Angkor, the surrounding city, fed by a vast irrigation network, may have held nearly a million people. The temple later became Buddhist and has never been abandoned.

events.title: Genghis Khan and the Mongol conquests
events.summary: Proclaimed Genghis Khan in 1206, Temüjin united the Mongol tribes and led them against northern China, Central Asia and Persia; his successors reached Kyiv, Baghdad, which they sacked in 1258, and all of China, completed by Kublai Khan in 1279. The largest contiguous land empire in history killed millions but then secured the trade routes across Eurasia, moving merchants, missionaries, paper money, printing and, in the fourteenth century, the plague. It fragmented into four khanates within a century.

events.title: Magna Carta
events.summary: At Runnymede in June 1215 rebellious barons forced King John of England to seal a charter limiting royal power: no free man was to be imprisoned or dispossessed except by the lawful judgment of his peers or the law of the land, and taxes required consent. It was annulled within months and reissued in revised form after John's death. Most of its clauses were feudal and specific, but its principle that the ruler is under the law became a touchstone for later constitutions.

events.title: The moai of Rapa Nui
events.summary: On Rapa Nui (Easter Island), the most isolated inhabited place on Earth, Polynesian settlers carved nearly a thousand monolithic figures from volcanic tuff between about 1250 and 1500 and moved statues weighing up to 80 tonnes kilometres from the quarry, most likely by 'walking' them upright with ropes, as experiments have shown. The old story of ecological suicide through deforestation has been challenged; disease and slave raids after European contact in 1722 did the greatest damage to the population.

events.title: Mansa Musa's pilgrimage from Mali
events.summary: Mansa Musa, ruler of the Mali Empire, travelled to Mecca in 1324 with a caravan of thousands and so much gold that its price in Cairo reportedly fell for years. The journey advertised West Africa's wealth to the Islamic world and to Europe, where Mali soon appeared on the Catalan Atlas. Musa returned with scholars and architects, and Timbuktu grew into a centre of Islamic learning whose manuscripts survive today.

events.title: Ibn Battuta's travels
events.summary: Leaving Tangier on pilgrimage in 1325, the Moroccan scholar Ibn Battuta travelled for nearly thirty years through North and East Africa, Arabia, Persia, Central Asia, India, where he served as a judge in Delhi, the Maldives, Sri Lanka, Southeast Asia and, he claimed, China, then across the Sahara to Mali. His Rihla, dictated on his return, is the fullest picture of the fourteenth-century Islamic world, though some passages are borrowed and some journeys doubted.

events.title: Vijayanagara, the great city of southern India
events.summary: Founded in 1336, the Vijayanagara Empire ruled most of southern India for two centuries from a capital at Hampi that Portuguese and Persian visitors described as among the largest and richest cities in the world, with markets of gems and horses and temples whose towers still stand. Its kings patronised Telugu, Kannada, Tamil and Sanskrit literature and Carnatic music. A coalition of Deccan sultanates defeated the empire at Talikota in 1565 and sacked the city.

events.title: The Black Death
events.summary: Bubonic plague, carried along Mongol trade routes from Central Asia, reached the Crimea in 1346 and spread by ship through the Mediterranean and across Europe, the Middle East and North Africa by 1353. It killed perhaps a third to a half of Europe's population and comparable shares elsewhere, the deadliest pandemic in recorded history. Labour shortages raised wages and loosened serfdom; persecutions of Jews and flagellant movements followed. Plague recurred in waves for four centuries.

events.title: The Italian Renaissance
events.summary: In fifteenth-century Florence, Venice and Rome, wealth from banking and trade paid for a revival of classical learning and a new art: Brunelleschi's dome and linear perspective, Donatello's and Michelangelo's sculpture, Leonardo's notebooks, Botticelli's and Raphael's painting, and Machiavelli's politics. Humanist scholars recovered Greek and Roman texts, many via Byzantine and Arabic transmission, and printing spread them. The Renaissance's celebration of human capacity, and its return to ancient sources, reshaped European thought.

events.title: Zheng He's treasure fleets
events.summary: Between 1405 and 1433 the Ming admiral Zheng He led seven expeditions of up to hundreds of ships and tens of thousands of men through Southeast Asia to India, Hormuz, Arabia and the East African coast, exchanging gifts, collecting tribute and bringing back a giraffe for the emperor. The largest ships were far bigger than any European vessel of the time, though their exact size is disputed. The voyages ended when the court turned inward, decades before Portuguese ships entered the Indian Ocean.

events.title: The Inca Empire at its height
events.summary: From 1438 under Pachacuti the Inca expanded from Cusco to rule about twelve million people along 4,000 kilometres of the Andes, the largest state in the pre-Columbian Americas. Without writing, wheels or iron, they administered it with quipu knot records, a 40,000-kilometre road system with relay runners, storehouses, terraced farming and labour tax, and built Machu Picchu. A civil war and smallpox, arriving ahead of the Spaniards, weakened the empire before Pizarro seized the emperor Atahualpa in 1532.

events.title: The Kingdom of Benin and its bronzes
events.summary: From the reign of Oba Ewuare around 1440, the Edo kingdom of Benin, in present-day southern Nigeria, built a walled capital whose earthworks were among the largest in the world and produced brass plaques and heads by lost-wax casting of a refinement that astonished Europe. Portuguese visitors traded with it from the 1480s. A British punitive expedition burned Benin City in 1897 and looted thousands of artworks, whose return from Western museums is the subject of continuing negotiation.

events.title: King Sejong creates the Hangul alphabet
events.summary: King Sejong of Joseon Korea devised Hangul, a featural alphabet whose letter shapes mirror the positions of the mouth and tongue, and promulgated it in 1446 in the Hunminjeongeum, explaining that the Chinese characters used by the elite were too hard for common people. The literati resisted it for centuries and it became Korea's official script only in the modern era. Linguists regard it as one of the most scientifically designed writing systems ever created.

events.title: Gutenberg's movable-type printing press
events.summary: Johannes Gutenberg of Mainz combined metal movable type, oil-based ink and a screw press into a practical system around 1450, printing his Bible by 1455. Movable type had been used in China since the eleventh century and in Korea, where metal type printed the Jikji in 1377, but Gutenberg's process suited the small alphabet of Latin script and spread rapidly. Within fifty years European presses had printed millions of volumes, transforming scholarship, religion and politics.

events.title: The Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy and its Great Law
events.summary: The Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga and Seneca nations united under the Great Law of Peace, attributed to the Peacemaker and Hiawatha; oral tradition and an eclipse mentioned in the founding story date it anywhere from the twelfth to the fifteenth century, so the date here is a placeholder within that range. The confederacy's council of chiefs, chosen by clan mothers, kept peace among its members for centuries and is cited, controversially, as an influence on American federalism.

events.title: The Ottomans take Constantinople
events.summary: On 29 May 1453 the army of the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II, using enormous bronze cannon, breached the walls of Constantinople and ended the Eastern Roman Empire after eleven centuries. The city became the Ottoman capital, Istanbul, and the empire went on to rule the Balkans, Anatolia, the Levant, Egypt and North Africa for four centuries. Greek scholars fleeing west carried manuscripts that fed the Renaissance, and the closing of overland routes gave Europeans a reason to seek the sea route to Asia.

events.title: Timbuktu under the Songhai Empire
events.summary: Sunni Ali took Timbuktu in 1468 and built the Songhai Empire along the Niger, which under Askia Muhammad from 1493 became the largest state in West African history. Its cities of Timbuktu, Djenné and Gao hosted scholars, courts and markets in gold, salt and books; the Sankore mosque and private libraries held hundreds of thousands of manuscripts on law, astronomy and medicine, many still surviving. A Moroccan army with firearms destroyed the empire at Tondibi in 1591.

events.title: Bartolomeu Dias rounds the Cape of Good Hope
events.summary: In early 1488 the Portuguese captain Bartolomeu Dias, blown south by a storm, turned east and found open water beyond the southern tip of Africa, proving that the Indian Ocean could be reached by sea. Decades of Portuguese voyages down the West African coast, driven by the search for gold and a route to Asian spices, had led to this point. Vasco da Gama followed the route to India in 1498, and Portugal built a maritime empire on it.

events.title: Columbus reaches the Americas
events.summary: On 12 October 1492 Christopher Columbus, sailing for Castile, landed in the Bahamas, opening sustained contact between Europe and the Americas. The continents had been inhabited for at least fifteen thousand years and Norse sailors had reached Newfoundland around 1000, so this was not a discovery for the people already there. Its consequences were global: the exchange of crops, animals and diseases, the collapse of Indigenous populations, and the Atlantic slave trade and colonial empires that followed.

events.title: Guru Nanak's teaching and the founding of the Khalsa
events.summary: Guru Nanak, born in Punjab in 1469, began teaching around 1499 that there is one God, that all people are equal regardless of caste or creed, and that honest work, sharing and remembrance of God are the path to liberation. Nine Gurus followed; the fifth compiled the scripture and built the Harmandir Sahib at Amritsar, and in 1699 the tenth, Gobind Singh, founded the Khalsa order, after which the scripture itself became the eternal Guru. Sikhs number about 25 million today.

events.title: The Safavids make Iran Shia
events.summary: In 1501 Ismail I, head of a Sufi order, took Tabriz and proclaimed himself shah, making Twelver Shia Islam the state religion of Iran, until then mostly Sunni, and importing Shia scholars from Lebanon and Iraq to teach it. Under Abbas I after 1588 the capital Isfahan became one of the world's most beautiful cities. The Safavid conversion created the Sunni-Shia divide between Iran and its Ottoman and Uzbek neighbours that still shapes Middle Eastern politics.

events.title: Luther's Ninety-five Theses and the Reformation
events.summary: In October 1517 the Augustinian friar Martin Luther circulated ninety-five theses attacking the sale of indulgences, an act tradition places on the door of the castle church at Wittenberg. His insistence on scripture and faith alone, spread by the new printing presses, split western Christianity into Catholic and Protestant churches, was taken up by Zwingli, Calvin and the English crown, and set off more than a century of religious wars. The Catholic Church answered with its own Counter-Reformation.

events.title: The first circumnavigation of the Earth
events.summary: Five ships left Spain under Ferdinand Magellan in 1519 seeking a western route to the Spice Islands; they found the strait at the tip of South America, crossed the Pacific, and Magellan was killed in the Philippines in 1521. Juan Sebastián Elcano brought the Victoria home in 1522 with eighteen survivors of about 270 men, completing the first voyage around the world. It demonstrated the true size of the Pacific and the globe and revealed the problem of the international date line.

events.title: The Ottoman Empire under Suleiman the Magnificent
events.summary: Suleiman I, sultan from 1520 to 1566, took Belgrade, Rhodes and most of Hungary, besieged Vienna in 1529, and extended Ottoman power over Iraq, the Red Sea and North Africa. Known in Turkish as the Lawgiver, he reorganised the empire's legal code; his architect Sinan built the Süleymaniye Mosque. The Ottoman state, a multi-religious empire ruling millions of Christians and Jews under the millet system, remained one of the world's great powers into the eighteenth century.

events.title: The fall of Tenochtitlan
events.summary: Tenochtitlan, the Aztec capital on an island in Lake Texcoco and one of the largest cities in the world, fell to Hernán Cortés on 13 August 1521 after a siege of three months. The Spaniards' several hundred soldiers were joined by tens of thousands of Indigenous allies, above all the Tlaxcalans, and by a smallpox epidemic that had killed the emperor Cuitláhuac. Mexico City rose on the ruins, and the conquest opened three centuries of Spanish rule in the Americas.

events.title: The transatlantic slave trade
events.summary: The first slave ship sailed directly from Africa to the Americas in 1526; the last documented voyage landed in Cuba in 1867. In between, European and American traders carried about 12.5 million enslaved Africans across the Atlantic, of whom nearly two million died at sea, to work plantations of sugar, tobacco and cotton in Brazil, the Caribbean and North America. It was the largest forced migration in history, devastated West and Central African societies, and shaped the demography and racial politics of the Americas.

events.title: Copernicus places the Sun at the centre
events.summary: Nicolaus Copernicus's On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres, printed in Nuremberg in 1543, the year of his death, argued that the Earth turns daily on its axis and orbits the Sun with the other planets. The model was mathematically no simpler than Ptolemy's at first, but it explained retrograde motion naturally and opened the way for Kepler's elliptical orbits and Galileo's telescopic evidence. The Church placed the book on the Index in 1616.

events.title: Vesalius's De humani corporis fabrica
events.wikipedia: De Humani Corporis Fabrica Libri Septem
events.summary: Andreas Vesalius, a Flemish physician teaching at Padua, published in 1543 an illustrated anatomy based on his own dissections of human bodies rather than on the ancient authority of Galen, whose descriptions had often come from animals. The Fabrica's precise woodcuts corrected hundreds of errors and set a new standard: knowledge of the body was to come from looking at the body. It appeared the same year as Copernicus's book, a coincidence often taken to mark the start of modern science.

events.title: Akbar's policy of religious tolerance in Mughal India
events.summary: The Mughal emperor Akbar, ruling from 1556 to 1605, abolished the jizya tax on non-Muslims in 1564, took Hindu Rajput princesses as wives, appointed Hindus to high office and from 1575 convened debates among Muslim, Hindu, Jain, Zoroastrian and Jesuit scholars at Fatehpur Sikri. His policy of sulh-i-kul, peace with all, made the Mughal state an empire of diverse subjects rather than a Muslim conquest state; it was reversed by his great-grandson Aurangzeb.

events.title: The Tokugawa shogunate closes Japan
events.summary: After Tokugawa Ieyasu became shogun in 1603, ending a century of civil war, his successors banned Christianity, expelled the Portuguese and by 1639 confined foreign trade to a Dutch post at Nagasaki and to Chinese, Korean and Ryukyuan channels. The policy later called sakoku kept Japan largely isolated from the West for over two centuries of internal peace, urban growth and flourishing arts, until American warships forced the ports open in 1853.

events.title: Galileo turns the telescope on the sky
events.summary: Having improved the newly invented Dutch telescope, Galileo Galilei published Sidereus Nuncius in March 1610, reporting mountains on the Moon, countless stars in the Milky Way and four moons circling Jupiter, proof that not everything orbits the Earth. His later observations of the phases of Venus supported Copernicus. Tried by the Inquisition in 1633 for defending the Sun-centred system, he spent his last years under house arrest, where he wrote his foundational work on motion and mechanics.

events.title: The Thirty Years' War and the Peace of Westphalia
events.summary: Beginning with a Protestant revolt in Bohemia in 1618, the war drew in Denmark, Sweden, France and Spain and devastated Germany, where perhaps a fifth of the population died of violence, famine and disease. The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 settled the religious map of the Holy Roman Empire and recognised the independence of the Dutch Republic and Swiss Confederation. It is often, if loosely, taken as the origin of the modern system of sovereign states.

events.title: Bacon, Descartes and the Royal Society
events.summary: Francis Bacon's Novum Organum of 1620 argued that knowledge of nature should be built up by systematic observation and experiment, and René Descartes's Discourse on the Method of 1637 by reasoning from clear first principles. The Royal Society of London, founded in 1660 with the motto 'take nobody's word for it', and the Académie des Sciences in Paris in 1666 institutionalised experiment, publication and peer scrutiny. Together they defined the methods that Newton's generation would use.

events.title: Leeuwenhoek observes microorganisms
events.summary: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, a Delft cloth merchant who ground tiny, powerful single lenses, reported to the Royal Society in 1676 that a drop of pepper water swarmed with 'little animals', the first observation of bacteria and protozoa. Robert Hooke's Micrographia of 1665 had already coined the word cell. Leeuwenhoek went on to describe red blood cells, sperm and muscle fibres. Their work revealed a living world invisible to the naked eye, though its link to disease waited two centuries.

events.title: Newton publishes the Principia
events.summary: Isaac Newton's Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica, published in London in 1687, set out three laws of motion and the law of universal gravitation, showing that the same force that pulls an apple to the ground holds the Moon and planets in their orbits. It unified terrestrial and celestial mechanics with mathematics and remained the framework of physics until Einstein. The book drew on Kepler, Galileo and Hooke, and on the calculus Newton and Leibniz developed independently.

events.title: The English Bill of Rights
events.summary: After the Glorious Revolution deposed James II, Parliament made William and Mary's accession conditional on a Declaration of Rights, enacted in December 1689. It forbade the monarch to suspend laws, levy taxes or keep a standing army without Parliament, guaranteed free elections and free speech in Parliament, and banned cruel and unusual punishments and excessive bail. It established parliamentary supremacy in Britain and was a direct model for the American Bill of Rights a century later.

events.title: The British Agricultural Revolution
events.summary: Over the eighteenth century English and Dutch farmers raised yields with crop rotations that replaced fallow with turnips and clover, selective breeding of livestock, enclosure of open fields, and tools such as Jethro Tull's seed drill of about 1701. Output per worker rose enough to feed growing cities and free labour for factories, a precondition of the Industrial Revolution. Enclosure also dispossessed many rural poor, and the balance between its gains and costs remains argued.

events.title: The steam engine, from Newcomen to Watt
events.summary: Thomas Newcomen's atmospheric engine of 1712 pumped water from English coal mines, the first practical machine to turn heat into work. James Watt's separate condenser, patented in 1769 and first installed commercially in 1776, cut its fuel use by three-quarters, and his rotary engines of the 1780s could drive mills and factories anywhere. Steam power freed industry from rivers and muscle, and its later applications to locomotives and ships transformed transport within a lifetime.

events.title: Linnaeus names the living world
events.summary: The Swedish naturalist Carl Linnaeus published Systema Naturae in 1735 and, in its tenth edition of 1758, gave every animal a two-word Latin name of genus and species, the binomial system still used for all organisms, and sorted them into a nested hierarchy of classes and orders. He placed humans among the primates as Homo sapiens. His classification was artificial in places and his ideas on human races have been repudiated, but his naming system made global biology possible.

events.title: The Encyclopédie and the Enlightenment
events.summary: Edited by Denis Diderot and Jean le Rond d'Alembert and published in 28 volumes between 1751 and 1772 despite censorship, the Encyclopédie set out to gather all human knowledge, from crafts and machines to philosophy, and to subject religion, government and tradition to reason. Its 70,000 articles by Voltaire, Rousseau, Montesquieu and others carried the Enlightenment's confidence in progress, tolerance and natural rights to readers across Europe and the Americas, preparing the ground for the revolutions that followed.

events.title: Mechanised cotton spinning and the factory
events.summary: James Hargreaves's spinning jenny of about 1764, Richard Arkwright's water frame patented in 1769 and installed in his Cromford mill in 1771, Samuel Crompton's mule of 1779 and Edmund Cartwright's power loom of 1785 mechanised textile production in Lancashire and Derbyshire. Cotton spun by machines in factories, fed by slave-grown American cotton and powered first by water and then steam, was the leading sector of the Industrial Revolution, which within a century remade work, cities and the world economy.

events.title: Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations
events.summary: Published in March 1776, Adam Smith's Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations explained how the division of labour raises productivity, how prices coordinate self-interested actors as if by an invisible hand, and why mercantilist restrictions on trade impoverish nations. It founded economics as a discipline and supplied the case for free markets and free trade, while also warning against monopolies and the deadening effect of repetitive work.

events.title: The United States Declaration of Independence
events.summary: Adopted by the Continental Congress on 4 July 1776 and drafted chiefly by Thomas Jefferson, the Declaration announced the separation of thirteen British colonies and asserted that all men are created equal, endowed with unalienable rights to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness, and that governments derive their just powers from the consent of the governed. Its author and many signers held slaves, a contradiction its later readers, from abolitionists to Lincoln, turned against slavery itself.

events.title: The US Constitution and Bill of Rights
events.summary: Drafted at Philadelphia in 1787 and in force from 1789, the Constitution created a federal republic with separated legislative, executive and judicial powers and is the oldest written national constitution still in use. The first ten amendments, the Bill of Rights, ratified in 1791, guarantee freedom of religion, speech, press and assembly, jury trial and due process. It counted enslaved people as three-fifths of a person for representation; the Thirteenth to Fifteenth Amendments after the Civil War began to repair that.

events.title: The French Revolution and the Declaration of the Rights of Man
events.wikipedia: Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen
events.summary: Weeks after the storming of the Bastille on 14 July 1789, the National Assembly adopted the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen, proclaiming that men are born free and equal in rights, that sovereignty lies in the nation, and that law is the expression of the general will. The Revolution abolished feudal privilege, executed the king, passed through the Terror and ended with Napoleon's coup in 1799; its declaration shaped constitutions and rights movements worldwide.

events.title: The Haitian Revolution
events.summary: Enslaved people in the French colony of Saint-Domingue rose in August 1791 and, under leaders including Toussaint Louverture and Jean-Jacques Dessalines, defeated French, Spanish and British forces over thirteen years. Haiti declared independence on 1 January 1804, the only state founded by a successful slave revolt and the second independent nation in the Americas. The revolution ended slavery there, alarmed slaveholding powers across the Atlantic world, and inspired abolitionists for decades.

events.title: Vaccination against smallpox
events.summary: Inoculation with material from smallpox pustules to induce a mild case had long been practised in China, India, the Ottoman Empire and West Africa, and was brought to Britain by Lady Mary Wortley Montagu in 1721 and to Boston by an enslaved man, Onesimus. In 1796 Edward Jenner showed that the milder cowpox protected against smallpox, a safer method he named vaccination. Vaccination programmes eradicated smallpox worldwide in 1980, the only human disease so far eliminated.

events.title: The Napoleonic Wars
events.summary: From 1803 to his final defeat at Waterloo in 1815, Napoleon Bonaparte's France fought successive coalitions across Europe, from Lisbon to Moscow, in wars that killed several million people. He redrew the map of the continent, spread the metric system and his civil code, and ended the Holy Roman Empire. His sale of Louisiana doubled the United States, and his occupation of Spain triggered the independence wars of Spanish America. The Congress of Vienna's settlement kept a general European peace for forty years.

events.title: Independence of Spanish America
events.summary: With Spain occupied by Napoleon, juntas across the Americas claimed self-rule from 1810. Fifteen years of war followed, led in the north by Simón Bolívar and in the south by José de San Martín, whose armies met in Peru; Mexico won independence in 1821 and the last royalist forces surrendered in 1826. Brazil separated peacefully from Portugal in 1822. Nearly all of the mainland Americas was independent by 1825, though slavery persisted in Brazil and Cuba for decades.

events.title: The first inter-city passenger railway
events.summary: The Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened on 15 September 1830, the first line to carry passengers and goods on a timetable between two cities entirely by steam locomotive, after George and Robert Stephenson's Rocket had won the Rainhill Trials the year before. A member of Parliament was killed by a train on opening day. Railways spread across Britain, Europe, India and the Americas within decades, collapsing distance, creating national markets and standard time.

events.title: Britain abolishes slavery in its empire
events.summary: Twenty-six years after outlawing the slave trade, Parliament passed the Slavery Abolition Act in August 1833, freeing about 800,000 enslaved people in the Caribbean, Mauritius and the Cape from 1834, though most were bound to years of unpaid 'apprenticeship' first, and slaveholders, not the enslaved, were paid compensation. It followed decades of campaigning by Black abolitionists such as Olaudah Equiano, mass petitions, and the 1831 uprising in Jamaica. France abolished slavery in 1848, the United States in 1865, Brazil in 1888.

events.title: The electric telegraph
events.summary: Cooke and Wheatstone in England and Samuel Morse in the United States patented working electric telegraphs in 1837; Morse's line from Washington to Baltimore opened in 1844 with the message 'What hath God wrought'. For the first time information travelled faster than a horse or a ship. The first lasting transatlantic cable was completed in 1866, and by the 1870s cables linked Europe to India, Australia and the Americas, wiring together markets, empires and newspapers.

events.title: The First Opium War
events.summary: When the Qing official Lin Zexu destroyed British opium at Canton in 1839, Britain sent a fleet whose steam gunboats and modern artillery overwhelmed Chinese defences. The Treaty of Nanking in 1842 ceded Hong Kong, opened five ports to foreign trade and residence and imposed an indemnity, the first of the 'unequal treaties'. The war began a century in which China lost sovereignty piece by piece to Western powers and Japan, a period Chinese historiography calls the century of humiliation.

events.title: Surgical anaesthesia
events.summary: On 16 October 1846 at Massachusetts General Hospital, William Morton administered ether while a surgeon removed a tumour from a patient's neck, the first public demonstration that surgery could be painless. Chloroform followed a year later in Edinburgh. Earlier claims exist, including Crawford Long's use of ether in 1842 and Hanaoka Seishū's herbal anaesthetic in Japan in 1804. Anaesthesia, with antisepsis two decades later, turned surgery from a desperate last resort into a routine treatment.

events.title: The Seneca Falls Convention and the Declaration of Sentiments
events.summary: The first women's rights convention, organised by Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott in Seneca Falls, New York, in July 1848, adopted a Declaration of Sentiments modelled on the Declaration of Independence: all men and women are created equal. Its most contested resolution demanded the vote. It launched the organised women's suffrage movement in the United States; New Zealand became the first self-governing country to grant women the vote in 1893, the United States in 1920.

events.title: The Taiping Rebellion
events.summary: Hong Xiuquan, a failed examination candidate who believed himself the younger brother of Jesus, led a millenarian movement that seized Nanjing in 1853 and ruled much of southern China as the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom, abolishing foot-binding and private landholding in principle. Qing armies, regional militias and Western-officered forces retook Nanjing in 1864. With an estimated twenty to thirty million dead from war, famine and disease, it was the deadliest civil war in history.

events.title: The Indian Rebellion of 1857
events.summary: Beginning with a mutiny of East India Company sepoys at Meerut in May 1857, the revolt spread across northern and central India, joined by princes, landowners and peasants with grievances against annexation, taxation and interference with religion. Delhi, Kanpur and Lucknow saw massacres on both sides before British forces prevailed in 1858. The Company was abolished and India placed under the Crown; the rebellion is remembered in India as the first war of independence.

events.title: Darwin publishes On the Origin of Species
events.summary: Charles Darwin's On the Origin of Species, published on 24 November 1859, argued that species change over time through natural selection acting on heritable variation, and that all living things share common ancestry. Alfred Russel Wallace had reached the same idea independently, prompting a joint announcement the year before. Evolution by natural selection became the unifying theory of biology, and its implications for human origins provoked religious and social debate that continues.

events.title: Germ theory of disease
events.summary: Louis Pasteur showed in 1861 that microorganisms cause fermentation and putrefaction and do not arise spontaneously; Joseph Lister applied the idea to surgery with carbolic antisepsis from 1867, and Robert Koch identified the bacteria of anthrax in 1876 and tuberculosis in 1882, setting out postulates for proving a microbe causes a disease. Ignaz Semmelweis had shown in 1847 that hand-washing prevented childbed fever, and was ignored. Germ theory underlies sanitation, vaccines and antibiotics.

events.title: The American Civil War and the end of slavery
events.summary: Eleven slaveholding states seceded after Abraham Lincoln's election, and war began at Fort Sumter in April 1861. Some 750,000 soldiers died, more than in all other American wars combined. The Emancipation Proclamation of 1863 declared enslaved people in rebel states free, nearly 200,000 Black men served in Union forces, and the Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery throughout the country in 1865, months after the Confederate surrender and Lincoln's assassination. Reconstruction's promise of equal citizenship was largely abandoned by 1877.

events.title: The Meiji Restoration
events.summary: In 1868 a coalition of samurai from Satsuma and Chōshū overthrew the Tokugawa shogunate and restored rule in the name of the young emperor Meiji. The new government abolished the feudal domains and samurai class, adopted a conscript army, universal schooling, railways, a Western-style constitution in 1889 and industrial policy, transforming Japan within a generation into the first non-Western industrial power, able to defeat China in 1895 and Russia in 1905.

events.title: Mendeleev's periodic table
events.summary: In 1869 Dmitri Mendeleev arranged the 63 known elements by atomic weight so that similar properties recurred at intervals, and left gaps for elements not yet found, predicting the properties of gallium, scandium and germanium, all discovered within fifteen years. Lothar Meyer reached a similar table independently. The periodic law was later explained by atomic structure and reordered by atomic number; the table remains chemistry's organising chart, with 118 elements today.

events.title: The telephone and electric lighting
events.summary: Alexander Graham Bell received a patent for the telephone in March 1876, hours ahead of Elisha Gray's filing; Antonio Meucci and others had built earlier devices, and priority remains argued. Thomas Edison's long-lasting carbon-filament lamp of 1879, and Joseph Swan's parallel work in England, made electric light practical, and Edison's Pearl Street station in New York began supplying customers in 1882. Electricity grids, motors and the telephone reshaped cities and work within a generation.

events.title: The Berlin Conference and the scramble for Africa
events.summary: Fourteen European states and the United States met in Berlin from November 1884 to February 1885 to set rules for claiming African territory; no African was present. Within twenty years almost the entire continent had been partitioned, often by force, with borders that cut across peoples and are largely those of today's states. The Congo Free State, King Leopold II's private domain recognised at Berlin, became notorious for atrocities that killed millions. Only Ethiopia and Liberia remained independent.

events.title: The automobile
events.summary: Karl Benz's Patent-Motorwagen, a three-wheeled carriage driven by a single-cylinder petrol engine, was patented in January 1886 and is generally counted the first practical automobile; Gottlieb Daimler and Wilhelm Maybach built a four-wheeled car the same year. Bertha Benz's 100-kilometre drive in 1888 was the first road trip. Henry Ford's moving assembly line of 1913 made cars affordable, and the automobile reshaped cities, landscapes, the oil industry and the atmosphere.

events.title: Brazil abolishes slavery
events.summary: On 13 May 1888 Princess Isabel signed the Lei Áurea, the Golden Law, freeing the roughly 700,000 people still enslaved in Brazil, the last country in the Americas to abolish slavery and the one that had received more enslaved Africans than any other, about four million.
