Abolition followed decades of flight, revolt and campaigning by Black and white abolitionists such as Luís Gama and Joaquim Nabuco. No compensation or land was provided to the freed; the monarchy fell the next year.

events.title: New Zealand grants women the vote
events.summary: On 19 September 1893 New Zealand became the first self-governing country to give all adult women, including Māori women, the right to vote in national elections, after petitions organised by Kate Sheppard gathered signatures from nearly a quarter of the adult female population. South Australia followed in 1894 and added the right to stand for parliament. Finland in 1906 was the first European country; most Western democracies enfranchised women after the First World War, Switzerland only in 1971.

events.title: Radioactivity and the Curies
events.summary: Henri Becquerel found in 1896 that uranium salts fogged photographic plates through paper; Marie and Pierre Curie showed the emission was a property of atoms, named it radioactivity, and in 1898 isolated two new elements, polonium and radium, from tonnes of pitchblende. Marie Curie won Nobel Prizes in physics and chemistry, the first person to win two. Radioactivity revealed that atoms could change, gave geologists a clock for the age of the Earth, and led to nuclear physics.

events.title: The first powered aeroplane flight
events.summary: On 17 December 1903 at Kill Devil Hills, North Carolina, Orville Wright flew the Wright Flyer for twelve seconds and 37 metres, the first sustained, controlled flight of a powered, heavier-than-air machine; the fourth flight that day lasted nearly a minute. The brothers' key insight was control in three axes, achieved by warping the wings. Within a decade aircraft crossed the Channel and served in war; within fifty years jet airliners crossed oceans in hours.

events.title: Einstein's annus mirabilis and special relativity
events.summary: In 1905, while working at the Swiss patent office, Albert Einstein published four papers: one explained the photoelectric effect with light quanta, one established the reality of atoms through Brownian motion, one introduced special relativity, in which space and time depend on the observer's motion and the speed of light is constant, and one derived the equivalence of mass and energy, E = mc². General relativity, his theory of gravity as curved spacetime, followed in 1915.

events.title: The Haber–Bosch process
events.summary: Fritz Haber demonstrated in 1909 that nitrogen from the air could be combined with hydrogen into ammonia under high pressure over an iron catalyst, and Carl Bosch scaled it to an industrial plant at Oppau by 1913. Synthetic ammonia made cheap fertiliser possible; roughly half the nitrogen in the bodies of people alive today has passed through the process, which sustains several billion of them. It also supplied explosives for two world wars, and Haber directed Germany's chemical warfare.

events.title: The Mexican Revolution
events.summary: A revolt against the thirty-year dictatorship of Porfirio Díaz in 1910 became a decade of civil war among factions led by Francisco Madero, Emiliano Zapata, Pancho Villa and Venustiano Carranza, in which perhaps a million people died. The Constitution of 1917 that emerged was among the first to guarantee social rights: land reform, an eight-hour day, the right to strike and national ownership of subsoil resources. It influenced constitutions across Latin America and beyond.

events.title: Amundsen reaches the South Pole
events.summary: Roald Amundsen and four companions reached the South Pole on 14 December 1911 using dog sleds and skis, techniques learned from Inuit and Sámi practice; Robert Falcon Scott's party arrived five weeks later and died on the return. The pole was the last of the great geographical goals on land. Its attainment closed the age of exploration that had begun with Polynesian and Portuguese navigators and left the deep sea and space as the remaining frontiers.

events.title: The Xinhai Revolution ends imperial China
events.summary: An uprising at Wuchang in October 1911 spread through the provinces, and in February 1912 the child emperor Puyi abdicated, ending the Qing dynasty and two thousand years of imperial rule. Sun Yat-sen briefly headed the new Republic of China before yielding to the general Yuan Shikai. The republic soon fragmented among warlords, but the revolution's ideas of nationalism and popular sovereignty shaped both the Nationalist and Communist movements that fought for China's future.

events.title: Plate tectonics is accepted
events.summary: Alfred Wegener proposed in 1912 that the continents had drifted apart from a single landmass, citing matching coastlines, fossils and rocks, but could offer no mechanism and was dismissed for decades. Mapping of the mid-ocean ridges, the discovery of sea-floor spreading by Harry Hess in 1962, and magnetic striping of the ocean floor led by 1968 to the theory of rigid plates moving over the mantle. Plate tectonics explains earthquakes, volcanoes, mountain building and the shape of the Earth's surface.

events.title: The First World War
events.summary: The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo in June 1914 set off a chain of mobilisations that brought the European alliances to war by August. Machine guns, artillery and trenches produced stalemate on the Western Front and slaughter at Verdun and the Somme; fighting spread to the Middle East, Africa and the seas, and colonial troops served in millions. Around nine million soldiers and several million civilians died. The war destroyed four empires and led to the Russian Revolution and the Second World War.

events.title: The Russian Revolution
events.summary: Bread riots and mutinies in Petrograd toppled Tsar Nicholas II in March 1917; in November Lenin's Bolsheviks seized power from the provisional government and took Russia out of the war. A civil war that killed millions ended with the Soviet Union established in 1922, the first state to attempt to build a socialist society. Its planned industrialisation, famines and terror under Stalin, victory over Germany and rivalry with the United States shaped the twentieth century until its dissolution in 1991.

events.title: The 1918 influenza pandemic
events.summary: An H1N1 influenza virus spread worldwide in three waves from early 1918, carried by troop movements at the end of the First World War. Estimates of the dead range from 17 to 50 million, possibly more, with India alone losing perhaps 12 million; unusually, young adults died in large numbers. Its origin is unknown; the name is an artefact of wartime censorship that spared neutral Spain's press. It remains the benchmark against which later pandemics are measured.

events.title: Quantum mechanics is formulated
events.summary: Between 1925 and 1927 Werner Heisenberg's matrix mechanics, Erwin Schrödinger's wave equation, Paul Dirac's synthesis and Max Born's probabilistic interpretation produced a complete theory of the atomic world, built on Max Planck's quantum of 1900 and Niels Bohr's atom of 1913. Heisenberg's uncertainty principle set limits on what can be known. Quantum mechanics explains chemistry, semiconductors, lasers and nuclear physics, and its interpretation is still argued a century on.

events.title: Penicillin and the antibiotic age
events.summary: Alexander Fleming noticed in September 1928 that a mould contaminating a culture plate at St Mary's Hospital, London, had killed the surrounding bacteria, and named its active substance penicillin. It was Howard Florey, Ernst Chain and Norman Heatley at Oxford who purified it and proved it cured infections in 1940–41, and American industry that mass-produced it by D-Day. Antibiotics have saved hundreds of millions of lives; resistance to them, which Fleming predicted, is now a global threat.

events.title: The Great Depression
events.summary: The Wall Street crash of October 1929 was followed by bank failures, collapsing trade and the deepest economic slump of the industrial era: US output fell by a quarter and unemployment reached a quarter of the workforce, with comparable distress in Germany, Latin America and beyond. Governments' responses ranged from Roosevelt's New Deal to the rise of the Nazis, who exploited German misery. The Depression discredited laissez-faire orthodoxy and produced Keynesian economics, welfare states and the institutions of Bretton Woods.

events.title: Gandhi's Salt March
events.summary: In March and April 1930 Mohandas Gandhi walked 390 kilometres from his ashram to the sea at Dandi and picked up a handful of salt, breaking the British monopoly and launching a nationwide campaign of civil disobedience in which some 60,000 people were jailed. It made satyagraha, non-violent resistance, the defining method of the Indian independence movement and a model for Martin Luther King Jr., Nelson Mandela and others. India became independent in August 1947, partitioned from Pakistan amid mass violence.

events.title: The Second World War
events.summary: The deadliest conflict in history began with Germany's invasion of Poland in September 1939, though war in Asia had opened with Japan's invasion of China in 1937. It ended in 1945 with Germany's surrender in May and Japan's in September after the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Estimates of the dead range from 70 to 85 million, including the six million Jews murdered in the Holocaust. The war reshaped borders, ended empires and created the United Nations.

events.title: The Holocaust
events.summary: Nazi Germany and its collaborators murdered about six million Jews, two-thirds of Europe's Jewish population, between 1941 and 1945 by mass shooting, starvation and gas in extermination camps such as Auschwitz and Treblinka, following years of persecution after 1933. Roma, disabled people, Soviet prisoners, Poles, political prisoners and gay men were also murdered in the millions. The Holocaust led to the Genocide Convention of 1948, the Nuremberg principle of individual responsibility, and shaped the modern idea of human rights.

events.title: Atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki
events.wikipedia: Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki
events.summary: On 6 and 9 August 1945 American aircraft dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, killing between 150,000 and 250,000 people, most of them civilians, by blast, fire and radiation. Japan surrendered on 15 August. The bombs, built by the Manhattan Project after the discovery of nuclear fission in 1938, were the first and so far only nuclear weapons used in war. The arms race that followed produced arsenals capable of ending civilisation, and treaties that have so far contained them.

events.title: The United Nations is founded
events.summary: Fifty nations signed the United Nations Charter in San Francisco in June 1945, and it entered into force on 24 October. Replacing the failed League of Nations, the UN committed members to settle disputes peacefully, to collective security through a Security Council with five permanent veto-holding members, and to human rights and self-determination. Its membership grew from 51 to 193 as colonies became states; its agencies eradicated smallpox, and its peacekeepers and courts have had mixed results.

events.title: Independence and partition of India and Pakistan
events.summary: British rule in India ended at midnight on 14–15 August 1947 with the creation of two states, India and Pakistan, the latter in two wings a thousand miles apart. Partition along hastily drawn religious lines uprooted some 14 million people and killed several hundred thousand to two million in communal massacres. It was the first great wave of decolonisation; within three decades most of Asia and Africa followed. Bangladesh separated from Pakistan in 1971 after a war and genocide.

events.title: The transistor
events.summary: On 16 December 1947 John Bardeen and Walter Brattain at Bell Labs demonstrated the point-contact transistor, a solid-state amplifier; William Shockley's junction transistor followed in 1948. Replacing fragile, power-hungry vacuum tubes, transistors made radios pocket-sized and computers reliable. Jack Kilby and Robert Noyce's integrated circuits of 1958–59 put many on one chip, and today a single processor holds tens of billions. The transistor is the most manufactured object in history and the foundation of the digital age.

events.title: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights
events.summary: The United Nations General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in Paris on 10 December 1948, with 48 votes in favour, none against and eight abstentions. Drafted by a committee chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt with members from China, Lebanon, France and elsewhere, its thirty articles assert rights to life, liberty, equality before the law, education and freedom of thought for every person. Not a treaty itself, it underpins later binding covenants and most national constitutions written since.

events.title: The Geneva Conventions of 1949
events.summary: Building on the first convention of 1864 inspired by Henry Dunant after the battle of Solferino, the four Geneva Conventions adopted on 12 August 1949 set binding rules for the treatment of wounded soldiers, shipwrecked sailors, prisoners of war and civilians in occupied territory, and a common article on internal conflicts. Ratified by every state in the world, they are the core of international humanitarian law, enforced by the International Committee of the Red Cross and, since 2002, the International Criminal Court.

events.title: The People's Republic of China is proclaimed
events.summary: After the Japanese surrender, civil war between Mao Zedong's Communists and Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalists resumed and ended with Communist victory; Mao proclaimed the People's Republic in Beijing on 1 October 1949 and the Nationalists withdrew to Taiwan. The new state redistributed land, then in the Great Leap Forward of 1958–62 caused a famine that killed tens of millions, and in the Cultural Revolution of 1966–76 tore its own society apart. Market reforms after 1978 lifted hundreds of millions from poverty.

events.title: The Korean War
events.summary: North Korean forces crossed the 38th parallel on 25 June 1950; a United Nations force led by the United States drove them back nearly to China, whose intervention pushed the front south again to a stalemate near the original line. The armistice of July 1953 has never been replaced by a peace treaty. Around three million people died, most of them Korean civilians. The war militarised the Cold War, fixed the division of Korea, and set the pattern for later proxy wars.

events.title: The structure of DNA
events.summary: In April 1953 James Watson and Francis Crick published the double-helix structure of DNA, drawing on X-ray diffraction images made by Rosalind Franklin and Raymond Gosling at King's College London, whose contribution was not properly credited for decades, and on Maurice Wilkins's work. The paired bases explained how genetic information is copied. The genetic code was cracked over the next decade, and the sequencing of the human genome, completed in 2003, followed from this structure.

events.title: The Bandung Conference
events.summary: Delegates from 29 newly independent Asian and African states, representing over half the world's population, met at Bandung, Indonesia, in April 1955, convened by Indonesia, India, Burma, Ceylon and Pakistan. They condemned colonialism and racism, affirmed the UN Charter's principles of sovereignty and self-determination, and sought a path between the Cold War blocs. The conference gave rise to the Non-Aligned Movement in 1961 and to the idea of the Third World as a political force.

events.title: The Vietnam War
events.summary: After the French defeat at Dien Bien Phu in 1954 and the partition of Vietnam, war between the communist North with its southern allies and the US-backed South escalated from 1955 to full American intervention in 1965, with over half a million US troops at its peak and bombing that spread to Laos and Cambodia. Between one and three million Vietnamese and 58,000 Americans died. Saigon fell in April 1975. The war reshaped American politics and the meaning of military power.

events.title: Ghana's independence opens Africa's decolonisation
events.summary: On 6 March 1957 the Gold Coast became Ghana under Kwame Nkrumah, the first sub-Saharan colony to win independence from a European power. In 1960 alone seventeen African states became independent, most of French and Belgian Africa among them. Where settlers resisted, as in Algeria, Kenya, Angola, Mozambique, Rhodesia and South Africa, independence or majority rule came only after long wars and struggles, the last, South Africa's first democratic election, in 1994.

events.title: Sputnik and the first human in space
events.summary: The Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite, from Baikonur in Kazakhstan on 4 October 1957, and on 12 April 1961 Yuri Gagarin became the first human to orbit the Earth. Both shocked the United States into a space race and the creation of NASA. Satellites soon carried weather observation, communications and navigation, and by the twenty-first century thousands orbited the Earth; the ballistic missiles that launched them were the delivery system of the nuclear age.

events.title: The oral contraceptive pill
events.summary: The US Food and Drug Administration approved Enovid as a contraceptive in June 1960, the result of research by Gregory Pincus and John Rock funded by Margaret Sanger and Katharine McCormick, and tested on women in Puerto Rico without full disclosure of risks. The pill gave women reliable control over fertility for the first time, altering family size, education, work and marriage patterns worldwide. Access spread unevenly and remains restricted in many countries.

events.title: The Second Vatican Council
events.summary: Convened by Pope John XXIII in October 1962 and closed by Paul VI in December 1965, the council of some 2,500 bishops reformed the Catholic Church, the world's largest religious institution: Mass in local languages rather than Latin, a declaration of religious freedom, dialogue with other Christians and other faiths, and the repudiation of the charge that Jews were collectively responsible for the death of Jesus. Its interpretation still divides Catholics between reformers and traditionalists.

events.title: The US Civil Rights Act and Voting Rights Act
events.summary: After a decade of boycotts, sit-ins, freedom rides and marches led by Martin Luther King Jr., Rosa Parks, John Lewis and thousands of others, and after the March on Washington of 1963, Congress passed the Civil Rights Act in July 1964, outlawing segregation in public places and discrimination in employment, and the Voting Rights Act in August 1965, banning the devices used to disenfranchise Black voters. They ended legal Jim Crow; the movement's methods inspired struggles for rights worldwide.

events.title: The Green Revolution
events.summary: High-yielding dwarf wheat bred by Norman Borlaug in Mexico and dwarf rice from the International Rice Research Institute in the Philippines, combined with irrigation, fertiliser and pesticides, roughly doubled cereal yields in India, Pakistan, Mexico and Southeast Asia from the mid-1960s, averting the famines then widely predicted. The gains bypassed much of Africa, favoured larger farmers, drew down aquifers and polluted waterways; the debate over its costs and benefits continues in every discussion of feeding the world.

events.title: ARPANET and the birth of the Internet
events.summary: The first ARPANET message passed between UCLA and Stanford Research Institute on 29 October 1969, over a network funded by the US Defense Department and built on packet switching, an idea developed by Paul Baran and Donald Davies. Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn's TCP/IP protocols, adopted across the network in January 1983, let separate networks connect into an internet. Tim Berners-Lee's World Wide Web of 1989–91 made it usable by anyone; today more than five billion people are online.

events.title: Humans land on the Moon
events.summary: On 20 July 1969 Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed the Apollo 11 lunar module Eagle in the Sea of Tranquility while Michael Collins orbited above; about 600 million people watched on television. Five more landings followed to 1972, returning 382 kilograms of rock that revealed the Moon's origin in a giant impact. The programme employed 400,000 people and answered Kennedy's 1961 challenge; no human has travelled beyond low Earth orbit since.

events.title: The Iranian Revolution
events.summary: Mass demonstrations and strikes drove Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi from Iran in January 1979, and Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini returned from exile to found an Islamic Republic ruled under the guardianship of the jurist, approved by referendum in April. The first modern revolution to establish a state on religious principles, it reshaped politics across the Muslim world, brought a US embassy hostage crisis, and was followed by an eight-year war with Iraq that killed hundreds of thousands.

events.title: Smallpox is eradicated
events.summary: The World Health Organization declared smallpox eradicated on 8 May 1980, three years after the last natural case in Somalia. A disease that had killed an estimated 300 million people in the twentieth century alone was ended by a global vaccination and surveillance campaign led by D. A. Henderson, with the largest efforts in India, Bangladesh and Ethiopia. It remains the only human disease deliberately eradicated; polio and Guinea worm are close.

events.title: The African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights
events.wikipedia: African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights
events.summary: Adopted by the Organisation of African Unity in Nairobi in June 1981 and in force from 1986, the Banjul Charter binds African states to civil and political rights and, distinctively, to economic, social and cultural rights, the rights of peoples to self-determination and development, and duties of individuals to family and community. It created the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights and, later, an African Court. It is the continent's own contribution to the international human rights system.

events.title: The Berlin Wall falls; the Cold War ends
events.summary: On 9 November 1989 East Germany opened the Berlin Wall after weeks of mass protest, following Poland's partly free elections and Hungary's opening of its border. Communist governments across Eastern Europe fell within months, mostly peacefully; Germany reunified in 1990, and the Soviet Union dissolved into fifteen states in December 1991. The Cold War, which had divided the world into rival blocs since 1947 and brought it to the brink of nuclear war in 1962, ended without a great-power war.

events.title: The Convention on the Rights of the Child
events.wikipedia: Convention on the Rights of the Child
events.summary: Adopted by the UN General Assembly on 20 November 1989, the Convention on the Rights of the Child recognises every person under eighteen as a holder of rights to survival, development, protection from violence and exploitation, education, and a voice in decisions affecting them. It is the most widely ratified human rights treaty in history, accepted by every UN member state except the United States. Its committee reviews each country's record every five years.

events.title: The Mabo decision recognises Aboriginal land rights
events.summary: On 3 June 1992 the High Court of Australia ruled in a case brought by Eddie Koiki Mabo and other Meriam people that native title to land had survived British colonisation, rejecting the doctrine of terra nullius, the claim that the continent had belonged to no one. Parliament's Native Title Act followed in 1993. The decision, and New Zealand's Waitangi Tribunal and Canada's constitutional recognition of Aboriginal rights, are part of a late-twentieth-century reckoning with Indigenous dispossession across the settler world.

events.title: South Africa's first democratic election
events.summary: From 26 to 29 April 1994 South Africans of all races voted together for the first time, ending apartheid, the system of legal racial segregation imposed in 1948. Nelson Mandela, released in 1990 after 27 years in prison, became president. The transition, negotiated between the African National Congress and the governing National Party after decades of resistance, international sanctions and township uprisings, was followed by a Truth and Reconciliation Commission and a constitution among the most rights-protective in the world.

events.title: The Rwandan genocide
events.summary: In about one hundred days from 7 April 1994, Hutu extremists in the government, army and militias murdered an estimated 500,000 to 800,000 Tutsi and moderate Hutu, often with machetes, while UN peacekeepers withdrew and the international community declined to intervene. The killing ended when the Rwandan Patriotic Front took the country in July. The genocide led to the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and to the doctrine of a responsibility to protect, adopted by the UN in 2005.

events.title: The human genome is sequenced
events.summary: The Human Genome Project, an international public effort begun in 1990, and the company Celera announced draft sequences in 2000 and the project declared the sequence essentially complete in April 2003, fifty years after the double helix; the last gaps were closed in 2022. Reading the three billion letters cost about three billion dollars; a genome can now be sequenced in hours for a few hundred. Genomics has transformed medicine, ancestry research and the study of human evolution.

events.title: The smartphone
events.summary: Apple's iPhone, announced in January 2007, combined a phone, an internet browser and a touchscreen computer in one pocket device; Android phones followed in 2008. Earlier smartphones from IBM, Nokia and BlackBerry existed, but the touchscreen and app model spread to most of humanity within fifteen years, with mobile networks bringing the internet to regions that never had fixed lines. The smartphone reshaped communication, commerce, news, photography and attention, for better and worse.

events.title: CRISPR gene editing
events.summary: In June 2012 Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier showed that the bacterial immune system CRISPR-Cas9 could be programmed with a short RNA to cut DNA at any chosen sequence, giving biologists a cheap, precise tool to edit genes; Feng Zhang's group demonstrated it in human cells months later, and patent disputes followed. The first CRISPR therapy, for sickle-cell disease, was approved in 2023. The 2018 editing of human embryos in China provoked worldwide condemnation and calls for limits.

events.title: The Paris Agreement on climate change
events.summary: On 12 December 2015, 196 parties to the UN climate convention adopted the Paris Agreement, committing to hold global warming well below 2 °C above pre-industrial levels and to pursue 1.5 °C, through nationally determined contributions reviewed every five years. It followed decades of climate science, from Svante Arrhenius's 1896 calculation to the IPCC's assessments. Its targets are not on track: warming passed 1.2 °C in the 2020s, and the treaty's success depends on national action it cannot compel.

events.title: The COVID-19 pandemic
events.summary: A new coronavirus, SARS-CoV-2, was identified in Wuhan, China, in December 2019 and declared a pandemic by the WHO in March 2020. Lockdowns halted much of the world's travel and economy; excess-death estimates run from about seven million confirmed to over twenty million in total by 2023, when the WHO ended the emergency. mRNA vaccines were developed and deployed within a year, a scientific first. The virus's precise origin remains under investigation.

events.title: mRNA vaccines
events.summary: Building on decades of work by Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman on modified messenger RNA and on lipid nanoparticle delivery, BioNTech with Pfizer and Moderna designed COVID-19 vaccines within days of the virus's genome being published in January 2020 and had them authorised by December, after trials showing about 95 percent efficacy. Billions of doses followed, though distribution to poorer countries lagged badly. The platform is now being applied to influenza, malaria and cancer.
